extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental investigators, and students of scientific method (readers of Baconian methodology)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance (from Bacon's Novum Organum and commentary) on designing experiments and inferring hidden/nonsensory causes from observable effects, including instruments, substitutions, gradations, and precautions against experimental artefacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction of non-sensible to sensible (deducuntur ad sensum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hidden qualities or operations of nature (that are not directly perceived) must be deduced to the sensible by careful, observable indications — 'haec maxime deducuntur ad sensum per notationes diligentes primorum incoeptuum et rudimentorum sive tentamentorum vitae'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe earliest inceptions and rudiments (e.g., animalcula from putrefaction, eggs, seedlings) and record minute notations of initial changes so that non-sensible actions (spirits, formative forces) become manifest through their effects on tangible parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use separation/distillation to analyse mixtures, but beware artefacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixtures of bodies ('Mistura Corporum') can be deduced to their components by artful and skilled separations (distillation, etc.), since nature of 'spiritus' and constituents appear via motions, corrosions, colours, odours, flavours after separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ artificiosa et peritae separationes to render components tangible. Anti-pattern: violent or abnormal processes (calores vehementes) may create new qualities not present originally — separation must not destroy or create the 'subtilioris schematismi' one seeks to detect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use weight (pondus) to deduce coacervation/density
rubrics_metrics.description: Coacervation and ratios of matter ('copiae materiae') are to be deduced to the sensible by weight: 'Pondus enim respondet copiae materiae...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile accurate tables of weights and volumes (specific gravities) for metals, minerals, woods, liquids, oils, etc., as a norm and operational standard (polychrestam) revealing variety among tangible bodies and allowing quantitative deductions about density and 'spiritus' content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify expansion / rarefaction by enclosed-volume experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperceptible expansions (of spirits, vapours) must be converted into measurable space by experiments (e.g., small glass phial + bladder assembly) to compute how much a body expands when vaporised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example protocol: fill small glass phial with spirit of wine, note weight with phial, fit a bladder over neck, heat over coals to distil into bladder, cool, measure remaining spirit weight and bladder volume; compare volumes to compute expansion ratios. Use small vessels to make evaporation with less heat; prevent recondensation by shaping the bladder top.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render imperceptible gradations (heat/cold) perceptible via transduced effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Degrees of calor and frigus that are too subtle for direct touch are to be deduced by their effects on air and subsequent effects on water/visible medium — e.g., the 'vitrum calendar' method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intermediate media/instruments (glass thermometer-like setups) where air expansion by heat depresses water and contraction by cold lifts it; observe water movement/level visually to infer gradations of temperature that the senses cannot directly feel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that artificial processes can introduce deceptive qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Many qualities observed under violent experimental conditions (ignis, strong agents) may be produced by the process itself and were not present in the original composite — 'plurimas qualitates... indi ab ipso igne... quae in composito prius non fuerunt; unde mirae fallaciae.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer mild, representative procedures that emulate nature; treat violent separations as potentially misleading. Record and consider whether observed qualities are genuine components or artefacts of the operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for latent processes occurring through time (latent process / instantiae viae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many natural motions are gradual and continuous and escape casual observation if one inspects only finished products; such 'instantiae viae' indicate nature's motus gradatim continuatos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe processes in operation and over time (be present during operation), or use devices/techniques that reveal slow changes (e.g., periodic daily checks, long-term observation). When direct observation is impractical, devise methods to aggregate or compute the slow motion (summas motus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle motions too slow or too fast for senses by aggregation or instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: If a motion is too slow to be perceived, deduce it by summation of motions or long-term records; if too fast, develop methods/instruments to measure or reduce velocity to measurable terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow motions: observe cumulative effects (summas motus) such as continental shifts or retreat of waterfalls. Fast motions: require invention of measuring techniques (astronomical eclipses, aberration of light, Fizeau/Foucault analogues) to bring them within measurable range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attenuate or distance noble/intense objects to permit perception
rubrics_metrics.description: When the nobility or intensity of an object (its strength) impedes the senses, apply elongation (distance), hebetation (interposed medium that weakens), reflection/admission/exception to avoid direct overpowering ('vel per elongationem majorcm... vel per hebetationem... vel per admissionem et exceptionem').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distance, absorbing/weakening media, or reflected/indirect presentation to reduce intensity so senses can perceive differences without being annihilated by the object’s strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for senses being overloaded by strong stimuli (limits of perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sense is so charged by an object that it cannot admit further impressions (especially olfaction), direct deduction may be impossible; recognize this limitation and use other routes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that some overloaded perceptions (particularly smell) cannot receive new admission; instead employ other senses, weaker stimuli, or analytical methods to obtain information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use other animals' senses or instruments when human senses are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: If human senses cannot detect a phenomenon (e.g., some odours or faint light), resort to animals whose senses exceed humans (dogs for odours; felids, noctuae for nocturnal light) or to instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage superior sensory capacities of animals or create/borrow instruments that extend human perception to detect phenomena latent to humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reasoning from anthropic analogy (lines of human analogy) without universal justification
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a major fallacy to constitute the lines/rules of things from the analogy of man rather than from the analogy of the universe — such errors are not corrected except by reason and universal philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize from human-perception-based analogies; correct and supplement sensory data with rational/phil osophical considerations and universal principles before inferring universal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substitution (Instantiae Supplementi) by gradation or analogue when sense is entirely destitute
rubrics_metrics.description: Where direct instances fail, supplement information by substitution either through gradation (finding media that gradationally attenuate an effect) or by analogy (comparable cases): 'Dupliciter autem fit substitutio; aut per Graduationem aut per Analoga.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when no medium entirely blocks magnetism, test various materials comparatively to find those that weaken magnetism in degrees (gold vs air vs silver hot/cold, etc.). Propose gradational experiments to reveal comparative effects even if no absolute blocker exists.
